summary: Published on April 1st, this humorous RFC proposes the "Two-Week Principle," a supposedly universal scale for estimating how long tasks take. Its joke is that, whatever the task, estimates tend to come out as about two weeks. It is satire about time estimation, not a real protocol.

eli5.summary: Ask almost anyone how long a job will take and they'll say "about two weeks." This joke document pretends that is a serious scientific rule.

questions: april fools rfc about time estimates
subtitle: Standardizing all time estimates to a universal duration of two weeks.

tldr.problem: Estimating time requirements for tasks remains a challenge across engineering, business, and everyday communication. Existing models fail due to unpredictability and inconsistencies in human estimation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9759 introduces the Two-Week Principle (TWP), which standardizes all temporal references to a single, uniform duration: two weeks. Every time estimate, regardless of original value or magnitude, is converted to two weeks.
tldr.outcome: This April Fools' RFC satirizes endemic problems with time estimation in software and engineering by proposing an absurdly consistent solution that treats time estimates as inherently meaningless and interchangeable.

today: RFC 9759 is an Informational RFC published on April 1, 2025. It remains the definitive satire of software project estimation practices and the universal tendency to answer time-related questions with "two weeks."

sections.title: The Universal Two-Week Estimate
sections.content: RFC 9759 is an April Fools' RFC that introduces the Two-Week Principle (TWP), a method for standardizing all time measurements into a universally accepted duration of two weeks. The document notes that engineers often underestimate development cycles, business leaders demand unreasonable turnaround times, and users expect instant results. The RFC proposes that all time-related units be mapped to two weeks, creating a universal standard that ensures clarity, predictability, and synchronization across all sectors relying on time-based scheduling.
sections.eli5: Whenever someone asks how long a task will take, the answer is always "two weeks." This is true whether it takes a second or a year in reality.

sections.title: Time Conversion and Implementation
sections.content: In TWP, all time estimates are mapped to two weeks: one second, five minutes, 24 hours, 3-5 business days, 6 months, 2 years, "ASAP", "it will be done when it is done", and any unlisted time value all convert to two weeks. The conversion table provides the standardized TWP duration in binary (100111011000000) and hexadecimal (0x4ec0) representations. Software must be updated to display "two weeks" instead of actual time values. Project management tools like Jira and ServiceNow should enforce two-week estimates for all tasks. Employees must be trained to reflexively respond to time questions with "two weeks". The iCalendar format must be updated to normalize all meeting timestamps to two weeks, with legacy software providing automated migration support.
sections.eli5: Every time estimate converts to two weeks. Whether someone asks "how long will this take?" or you look at a calendar, the answer is always two weeks. Software and calendars must be updated to show this.

sections.title: Quantum Effects and Security
sections.content: The RFC addresses theoretical implications for quantum computing, noting that quantum uncertainty could make TWP a stabilization factor for quantum timekeeping, reducing complex error correction. However, quantum implementations must not employ multiple instances of TWP within a scaling variable, as this could introduce temporal feedback instabilities and lead to accidental wormhole creation, an outcome outside the RFC's scope. Remarkably, the security considerations section asserts that there are no security concerns: any vulnerabilities discovered in TWP will be fixed in two weeks. The RFC strongly recommends immediate implementation to standardize time estimation and eliminate stress, miscommunication, and disappointment.
sections.eli5: The RFC jokes that quantum computers might use the two-week principle to fix timing errors. It also jokes that if there are any security problems, they will be fixed in two weeks.
